responses.response: Use four primary deployment tiers. `#Dmz`: API gateway/edge ingress only; TLS termination, routing, WAF/rate limiting; inbound allowed from the Internet, outbound allowed only to `#AppTier`, and no direct access to data stores. `#AppTier`: business services and synchronous APIs; authentication, validation, orchestration, document workflow decisions; accepts traffic only from `#Dmz` or trusted internal callers, may publish to RabbitMQ, and may access approved data services. `#ProcTier`: async worker(s) and, if it is dedicated to this processing flow, RabbitMQ; queueing, retries, document conversion/OCR/indexing, background jobs; no public ingress, accepts messages from `#AppTier`, and can write results to `#DataTier`. `#DataTier`: MongoDB and MinIO; durable metadata/content storage, backup/restore, replication; private inbound only from `#AppTier` and `#ProcTier` on required ports, never from `#Dmz`. Monitoring is usually cleaner as a sibling shared observability zone or a separate focused view because it is cross-cutting rather than a core business tier.

No. This skill should primarily define the tier structure, what belongs in each tier, and the allowed communication matrix. It can show light illustrative examples, but exact VM names, Markdown spec tables, and detailed `Node_App { instanceOf ... }` wiring are downstream deployment-detail work. A good boundary is: this skill answers which tier/zone an element belongs to and who may talk to whom; node naming, per-VM inventories, and concrete instantiation belong to the next level of infrastructure modeling.

Keep the main `Dmz`/`AppTier`/`ProcTier`/`DataTier` stack intact and add both concerns as peers rather than forcing them inside one existing tier. Put the cross-cutting audit/security capability in a sibling shared zone next to the main tiers, tagged for security/shared infrastructure, because multiple tiers emit audit events or consume security services; connect only the needed flows and avoid duplicating the same service inside every tier. Model the standby disaster-recovery site as a separate site/environment at the same hierarchy level as primary production, with a mirrored reduced tier stack or only the standby tiers that actually exist; tag it for recovery/backup and show replication/failover links between primary and DR counterparts. For readability, prefer one primary-tier overview, one focused security/audit view, and one DR/failover view instead of one overloaded diagram.
